questions.prompt: What makes group chat a distinct distraction problem in this chapter?
choices: It combines fast message flow with visible pressure to respond or stay present
It is identical to email in every way
It only causes problems when there are too many emojis

explanation.gentle: Chat adds social visibility and response pressure.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats group chat as a visible-responsiveness trigger loop.
explanation.competitive: It is a ping with a crowd.

questions.prompt: Why are norms more important than the app alone here?
choices: Because the group decides whether a message means urgent attention or ordinary discussion
Because settings never matter at all
Because chat apps cannot be changed

explanation.gentle: The group gives the message its social meaning.
explanation.direct: Norms determine whether chat coordinates or distracts.
explanation.competitive: Culture tells the ping what badge to wear.

questions.prompt: Why can silence in chat feel so heavy?
choices: Because response and presence are socially visible in a shared space
Because chat messages are always emergencies
Because people can never contribute asynchronously

explanation.gentle: People often feel they are being seen for how quickly they respond.
explanation.direct: Visible presence pressure makes delay feel more loaded than in email.
explanation.competitive: The audience raises the price of silence.

questions.prompt: Which of these fits the chapter's solution?
choices: Giving channels clear purpose and separating urgent use from routine discussion
Treating every chat as a live emergency lane
Using chat with no muting or response expectations at all

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants clearer jobs and urgency rules for channels.
explanation.direct: Boundaries and purpose make chat more governable.
explanation.competitive: Write the constitution before the chaos writes one.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter endorse muting only alongside expectation changes?
choices: Because technical controls fail if the culture still treats delayed response as suspicious
Because muting never helps under any circumstances
Because people should always stay visibly available

explanation.gentle: The norm around delay has to change too.
explanation.direct: A mute button needs cultural permission behind it.
explanation.competitive: The button loses if the norm keeps prosecuting silence.

questions.prompt: A team uses one channel for incidents, casual updates, and brainstorming. What is the chapter's stronger diagnosis?
choices: Mixed channel purpose lets routine messages borrow urgency and keeps everyone half-alert
The team needs even more notifications
All chat should be replaced with meetings immediately

explanation.gentle: The channel is mixing different stakes together.
explanation.direct: Purpose confusion lets chat borrow urgency from itself.
explanation.competitive: One room is trying to wear every badge.

questions.prompt: What mistake does the chapter avoid by distinguishing chat from email?
choices: Ignoring the extra pressure created by visible presence and response optics
Pretending email is more public than chat
Saying message volume never matters

explanation.gentle: Chat has a stronger social-pressure layer than email.
explanation.direct: The chapter keeps chat distinct by centering visibility and real-time norms.

questions.prompt: What limit does the chapter preserve?
choices: Chat can still be useful when it has purpose, urgency rules, and boundaries
All group chat is always harmful
Useful coordination only happens in meetings

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants better governance, not abolition.
explanation.direct: Bounded chat can still coordinate effectively.
explanation.competitive: Do not torch the tool because the rules were sloppy.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter connect to the email chapter before it?
choices: It keeps the trigger logic but shifts from inbox ambiguity to visible real-time social pressure
It says email and chat should be handled identically
It abandons the communication theme altogether

explanation.gentle: The same attention problem becomes faster and more social here.
explanation.direct: The chapter intensifies the earlier logic by centering visibility and pace.
explanation.competitive: The trigger loop gets an audience.

questions.prompt: Why does the next chapter move into meetings?
choices: Because unresolved chat pressure often spills into calendar grabs and more synchronous time claims
Because meetings are calmer than chat in every possible case
Because group chat has nothing to do with coordination

explanation.gentle: Loose chat norms often push uncertainty onto the calendar.
explanation.direct: Meeting overload can grow out of unresolved real-time coordination pressure.
explanation.competitive: Channel chaos starts renting conference rooms.
